Reasoned native-loader review, 2026-10-19

Original samples (SHA-256):
d436eab3d7eeb00dd72ed9fde0e1c989b495cc801aad1558728e8e5a4aed0f88
b3308799ef35cbc01ec48eb6325e236ed130b83312cb041a6129a928422c8a0d
6afd8a7a81a2bb7011437a084a92cd470388dc8b3a270c2ad8c19673470e59b8

All three are MALICIOUS based on code, not their collection filenames or ML.
No fetched dependency is implicated. Samples were not executed on the host.

myRunner / QQpass-associated backdoor (d436):
MFC PE, HanSoft myRunner version resource. At VA 0x406465 it creates the HKLM
Software\Classes\exefile\shell\open\command key. The 0x40650f path strips
the wrapper's extension, appends the quoted %1 / %* argument template and
writes through helper 0x404610 (RegSetValueExA). POP3 retrieval at 0x40919e
feeds attachment decoding, .exe selection and a nine-byte X-tag check at
0x40923e. The unversioned attachment path reaches WinExec at 0x4092f2;
numbered filenames also use a registry version gate. This is association
hijacking and mailbox-controlled payload execution, not WannaCry/GlassWorm
ransomware merely because the collector put those names in its filename.
Existing behavioral detections are justified; no sample-specific rule change.

Blihan HTTP task/payload loader (b330):
Readable code remains in MPRESS-labelled sections; labels do not prove that
this image needs unpacking. Rizin instruction decoding reported invalid sites
that Capstone and direct byte checks decode normally (e.g. VA 0x4011fd).
Startup reads its own image, copies it to Windows\microsofthelp.exe, writes
HKCU's CurrentVersion\Run value through 0x401a70 and starts the copy.
0x401270 repeatedly fetches a response via 0x4017c0. It checks length >0x54
and magic 0x1e240 at response+0x40, XORs the record body at +0x48 using its
first 64 bytes as a cycling key (0x401490), then selects typed records through
0x4014d0. GetAdaptersInfo supplies six MAC bytes used in an HTTP query.
The polling thread at 0x401930 dispatches type 0x200 to 0x401610. That handler
fetches a PE, checks MZ, writes it to a generated eight-letter .exe beside
itself, closes it, and calls the CreateProcessA wrapper at 0x401e00.
Other records drive hidden Internet Explorer visits and delays. The embedded
HidePlugin.dll is loaded and WindowsHookExON is resolved/called (0x4015c4).
That export name does not establish injection or credential/key theft.
The image reads a configuration offset from DOS header +0x1c; this specimen
has zero there, so its operational endpoint cannot be recovered honestly
from this path. Appended UTF-16 sandbox/executable paths are padding, not a
list of files it actually accesses. No ransomware or secret exfiltration
path was established. Keep concrete tasking, persistence and payload-launch
traits, remove redundant hostile padding composites, and describe Blihan
as a backdoor loader rather than assert an unobserved stealer role.

Mirai DLR native downloader (6afd):
ARM32 static OABI ELF. Entry 0x831c jumps to 0x8178. It prints MIRAI, creates
an output with flags 0x241 and mode 0777 at 0x81dc, opens a TCP socket and
connects to 185.228.72.128:80. It sends GET /jklarm5 HTTP/1.0, shifts a byte
at a time until CRLFCRLF (0x826c), then reads into a 128-byte stack buffer
and writes that same buffer/count to the output descriptor (0x829c).
It closes both descriptors, prints FIN and exits with status 5. There is no
execve, shell, scanning, DDoS, or persistence in this downloader itself.
This matches the published Mirai dlr/main.c control flow, syscall wrappers,
status protocol and file mode, with changed endpoint/path. Source:
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jgamblin/Mirai-Source-Code/master/dlr/main.c
A generic small static HTTP/0777 client is now notable, not hostile.
Family rules require the DLR protocol and staging evidence. Ordinary OABI
socket/connect wrappers are notable. Filename and endpoint are not required.

Placement / preservation:
- Generic tiny HTTP+0777 co-occurrence: objectives/.../staging/stager ->
  micro-behaviors/communications/http/download/executable. Matcher unchanged;
  hostile -> notable is an intentional precision correction. Its one exact
  consumer follows the move. The existing renamed ARM fixture has the
  open-mode atom but no matching network-wrapper pair; its stale expected
  hostile composite is corrected to assert that atom and no Mirai identity.
- Record header byte fingerprint: C2 -> metadata/binary/instruction/sequence;
  section scope widened from MPRESS1 to mapped sections. Magic/length checks
  alone do not establish attacker control.
- Existing inline 64-byte XOR loop: crypto/symmetric/xor/loop ->
  data/encoding/xor, preserving matcher/scope/confidence. The routine both
  decodes and restores records. No old exact-ID or bare ancestor consumers
  selected this atom. The C2 rule now requires it explicitly.
- Blihan identity subtree: stealer -> backdoor, all atoms retained. Names and
  descriptions no longer claim theft or injection. No external YAML consumers
  selected this subtree. Run-key and payload objectives are separate.

Validation controls:
Mutation-based tests preserve original code while removing one independently
required role. Remove MIRAI or FIN, or change open mode to 0644: neither Mirai
hostile rule may fire. Rename the output: both must still fire. Change the
XOR key-wrap bound: HTTP task and file-launch composites must stop. Change
the word-gated file handoff branch: only the file-launch composite must stop.
Original samples retain respectively 4, 4 and 2 hostile traits. The Blihan
count spans tasking, file execution, login persistence and family identity.

Isolated instruction emulation (Unicorn, mocked syscalls only) confirmed the
ARM socket endpoint, request bytes, mode 0777, exact response-body write,
MIRAI/FIN stdout, and exit 5. The original Blihan key64 XOR routine was also
emulated on a synthetic record: one pass transformed the body and a second
restored it. These checks performed no real network or filesystem operations.
